title: Robotaxis are expanding faster than they can fix their problems
excerpt: Robotaxi companies are scaling their operations as they continue to run into driving scenarios that could trip up the AI driver.
content_html:
Robotaxis are scaling now, fixing problems later

By Lloyd Lee

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Every now and then, I entrust my life to an AI.

That AI — a Waymo robotaxi — has increasingly become a legitimate means of mobility for some here in San Francisco.

By now, I rarely worry if I'll get home safe, but I still pay attention.

Waymo and other robotaxi companies say their data prove their AIs are much safer than human drivers. In the hundreds of miles I've traveled with Waymo, I've never encountered a safety incident that required human intervention.

That's not to say robotaxis are perfectly safe. They're still running into issues most human drivers are accustomed to, like navigating construction zones.

And safety is only part of the equation for a seamless ride-hailing service. I've witnessed firsthand the smaller quirks that come with the driverless experience.

Soon, people outside the world's tech hubs will get a chance to see them, too.

The robotaxis are coming

The robotaxi industry in the past month has been busy scaling operations.

On Tuesday, Waymo opened its Dallas service to the public after initially limiting rides to waitlisted users. The company said nearly 150,000 people have tried Waymo since February.

Amazon-owned Zoox announced Wednesday that it plans to begin charging for rides in Las Vegas, signaling that the service is maturing as it goes commercial.

In Florida and Texas, Tesla added new service areas for its Robotaxi. In some regions, the company has started offering a limited number of unsupervised rides.

Robotaxi companies are also expanding beyond the US. Uber and UK-based Wayve said on Wednesday that they received regulatory approval to start offering supervised autonomous rides in London this summer. Waymo also plans to launch a commercial service in London by the end of the year.

Way more Waymos, way more problems?

The rapid pace of scaling can give the impression that robotaxi companies are confident that autonomy has largely been solved.

Phil Koopman, an AV safety expert and emeritus professor of electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, said the reality is more complicated, and the more these robotaxis scale, the more so-called edge cases they'll run into.

"When you have a hundred cars, you're at the threshold where stuff that used to be so rare you could ignore it, you can't ignore it anymore," Koopman told Business Insider.

Waymo, the leading robotaxi provider in the US, demonstrated that tension.

In May, the company suspended freeway rides after it said that it was trying to improve how the vehicles behaved around construction zones. Freeway rides are critical if Waymo wants to cash in on longer, more lucrative trips, such as airport routes.

Last week, Waymo gradually restored its freeway service following company-issued software updates, providing a stark example of how a robotaxi provider can disable a feature deployed for real-world passengers to resolve a newly discovered issue.

A Waymo spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

AVs also still trip up in the face of a major city's disorder and chaos.

Videos posted online show how Waymo vehicles can sometimes obstruct emergency-response scenes. Waymos were also immobilized amid heavy traffic in San Francisco on the Fourth of July.

The problems have been persistent enough for SF's pro-tech mayor, Daniel Lurie, to call for stricter statewide regulations last month.

Those calls have extended to the federal level, where regulators from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration warned of the pitfalls autonomous vehicles still face in active emergency scenes.

NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison wrote in a July 8 letter to AV developers that the federal agency has documented a "clear pattern of driverless AVs interfering with law enforcement and other first responders."

"The question is, as they expand, can they fix [the problems] as fast as they find them?" Koopman said. "And with floods and construction zones and a bunch of other things, the answer is they haven't been able to fix them."

The small quirks of going driverless

Ensuring that a robotaxi doesn't obstruct an ambulance is a serious issue.

There can also be smaller, mostly inconsequential quirks in a robotaxi ride that may not always warrant a formal report to a regulatory body.

In a video posted on X by Tesla fan David Moss, a human safety monitor of a Tesla Robotaxi in San Francisco could be seen waiting for the car to merge back into traffic for about a minute before eventually taking control of the wheel.

Those interventions aren't captured under the same public reporting framework that applies to Waymo's driverless service through the California Public Utilities Commission, the state agency that regulates passenger transportation services.

A Tesla spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

In an op-ed published in The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday, an attorney recounted an unsettling Waymo experience in which the robotaxi inexplicably made a turn in the wrong direction. The rider said he and his wife essentially ejected themselves from the ride after the Waymo "shuddered to a stop."

The attorney wrote how a Waymo rep told them there was nothing that could be done.

Koopman said riders should expect autonomous vehicles to sometimes do inexplicably "weird things."

"Anyone who expects this technology to be perfect or always do exactly the same thing, you're in for disappointment," he said, adding that the safety challenge is making sure those strange behaviors remain benign.

I've never experienced some of the serious cases that other riders have reported — being driven in the middle of a flood or creeping through an active crime scene.

On an evening last December, I hailed a Waymo to get back home from downtown San Francisco.

My ride was pleasantly uneventful, as I hope every robotaxi ride will be. Until the Waymo driver made a mistake.

The car drove past the right turn into my house and made a left up the road, taking me in a circle around the neighborhood before it got back on track and delivered me home.

It was harmless, but curious.

I have no idea why the Waymo did that. All I could do was let the AI take the wheel.

content_html_zh:
Robotaxis 现在正在扩展，稍后解决问题

作者：Lloyd Lee 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

我时不时地将自己的生命托付给人工智能。

对于旧金山的一些人来说，人工智能——Waymo 机器人出租车——已经日益成为一种合法的出行方式。

到现在为止，我很少担心是否能安全回家，但我仍然会注意。

Waymo 和其他机器人出租车公司表示，他们的数据证明他们的人工智能比人类司机安全得多。 在我与 Waymo 一起行驶的数百英里中，我从未遇到过需要人工干预的安全事件。

这并不是说机器人出租车完全安全。 他们仍然遇到大多数人类司机都习惯的问题，比如在施工区行驶。

安全只是无缝乘车服务的一部分。 我亲眼目睹了无人驾驶体验带来的一些小怪癖。

很快，世界科技中心以外的人们也将有机会看到它们。

机器人出租车来了

过去一个月，机器人出租车行业一直忙于扩大业务规模。

周二，Waymo 向公众开放了达拉斯服务，此前该服务最初仅限于等候名单上的用户。 该公司表示，自 2 月份以来已有近 15 万人尝试过 Waymo。

亚马逊旗下的 Zoox 周三宣布，计划开始在拉斯维加斯开始收费，这表明该服务随着商业化而日趋成熟。

在佛罗里达州和德克萨斯州，特斯拉为其机器人出租车增加了新的服务区域。 在一些地区，该公司已开始提供数量有限的无人监管乘车服务。

机器人出租车公司也在向美国以外的地区扩张。 Uber 和总部位于英国的 Wayve 周三表示，他们已获得监管部门批准，将于今年夏天开始在伦敦提供受监管的自动驾驶服务。 Waymo 还计划于今年年底在伦敦推出商业服务。

Waymos 越多，问题就越多吗？

规模的快速扩张给人的印象是，机器人出租车公司对自动驾驶问题已基本得到解决充满信心。

AV 安全专家、卡内基梅隆大学电气与计算机工程名誉教授菲尔·库普曼 (Phil Koopman) 表示，现实情况更为复杂，这些机器人轴规模越大，遇到的所谓边缘情况就越多。

库普曼告诉《商业内幕》：“当你拥有一百辆汽车时，你就处于一个门槛，以前非常罕见的东西你可以忽视它，但你不能再忽视它了。”

美国领先的机器人出租车提供商 Waymo 就展现了这种张力。

今年五月，该公司表示正在努力改善车辆在建筑区域周围的行为，因此暂停了高速公路行驶。 如果 Waymo 想要在机场路线等更长、更有利可图的行程中获利，高速公路出行就至关重要。

上周，Waymo 在公司发布软件更新后逐渐恢复了高速公路服务，这提供了一个鲜明的例子，说明机器人出租车提供商如何禁用为现实世界乘客部署的功能来解决新发现的问题。

Waymo 发言人没有回应置评请求。

面对大城市的无序和混乱，自动驾驶汽车仍然会出现故障。

网上发布的视频显示 Waymo 车辆有时会阻碍紧急响应场景。 7 月 4 日，由于旧金山交通拥堵，Waymos 也陷入瘫痪。

这些问题一直持续存在，以至于旧金山的亲科技市长丹尼尔·卢里 (Daniel Lurie) 上个月呼吁在全州范围内实施更严格的监管。

这些呼吁已经扩展到联邦层面，美国国家公路交通安全管理局的监管机构警告说，自动驾驶汽车在紧急情况下仍然面临着陷阱。

NHTSA 局长乔纳森·莫里森 (Jonathan Morrison) 在 7 月 8 日致自动驾驶汽车开发商的一封信中写道，该联邦机构已经记录了“无人驾驶自动驾驶汽车干扰执法和其他急救人员的明显模式”。

“问题是，随着他们的扩张，他们能尽快解决[问题]吗？” 库普曼说道。 “对于洪水、建筑区和其他一系列问题，答案是他们无法解决这些问题。”

无人驾驶的小怪癖

确保机器人出租车不会妨碍救护车是一个严重的问题。

机器人出租车出行中也可能存在一些较小的、大多是无关紧要的怪癖，这些怪癖可能并不总是需要向监管机构提交正式报告。

在特斯拉粉丝大卫·莫斯 (David Moss) 在 X 上发布的一段视频中，可以看到旧金山一辆特斯拉自动驾驶出租车的人类安全监视器等待汽车重新融入车流约一分钟，然后最终控制了方向盘。

这些干预措施并未通过加州公共事业委员会（监管客运服务的州机构）适用于 Waymo 无人驾驶服务的相同公共报告框架来体现。

特斯拉发言人没有回应置评请求。

在周二《华尔街日报》发表的一篇专栏文章中，一位律师讲述了一次令人不安的 Waymo 经历，其中机器人出租车莫名其妙地转向了错误的方向。 这名骑手表示，在 Waymo“颤抖着停下来”后，他和他的妻子基本上从车里跳了出去。

律师写道，Waymo 代表告诉他们无能为力。

库普曼表示，乘客应该预料到自动驾驶汽车有时会做出莫名其妙的“奇怪的事情”。

他说：“任何期望这项技术完美或总是做同样事情的人都会失望。”他补充说，安全挑战是确保这些奇怪的行为保持良性。

我从未经历过其他骑手报告的一些严重案件——在洪水中开车或爬过活跃的犯罪现场。

去年 12 月的一个晚上，我叫了一辆 Waymo 从旧金山市中心回家。

我的旅程非常顺利，我希望每次机器人出租车之旅都如此。 直到Waymo司机犯了一个错误。

汽车驶过右转口进入我家，然后向左拐上路，带我在附近绕了一圈，然后又回到正轨并送我回家。

它无害，但很好奇。

我不知道 Waymo 为何这么做。 我所能做的就是让人工智能来掌舵。
